Finding: AES_KEY_SHARE0/1 and AES_DATA_IN registers return real key/data on MMIO read instead of hardwired 0; raw AES key can be read back and both shares XORed to recover it in the clear.
Detection method: Static diff vs upstream caliptra-rtl v2.1.2 (evidence/01_...diff); manual datapath trace of reg2hw.key_share0/1.q into reg_rdata_next
Security impact: Complete disclosure of AES key material to any software/DMA agent with register read access; breaks confidentiality of any secret protected by the hardware AES engine (incl. OCP-Lock/DICE-derived keys)
Adversary profile: Local software/firmware executing on the SoC with MMIO read access to the AES peripheral; no elevated privilege required
Proposed mitigation: Restore hardwired 0 return for KEY_SHARE0/1 and DATA_IN read paths in the auto-generated reg_top (fix reggen template/RDL and regenerate); add SVA that these addresses always read 0
Exploit code: for i in range(8): key_share0[i]=mmio_read32(AES_KEY_SHARE0_BASE+4*i); key_share1[i]=mmio_read32(AES_KEY_SHARE1_BASE+4*i); key=[a^b for a,b in zip(key_share0,key_share1)]

Security feature bypassed: REGWEN-gated write lock on AES auxiliary control
Finding: ctrl_aux_shadowed_gated_we no longer ANDed with ctrl_aux_regwen_qs; CTRL_AUX_SHADOWED (incl. key_touch_forces_reseed) stays writable forever, even after firmware clears the REGWEN lock.
Security impact: Attacker/malicious code can re-enable or weaken AES SCA hardening settings after boot-time lockdown, undermining the write-once security configuration model
Adversary profile: Local software with MMIO write access to the AES peripheral after boot lock was supposed to take effect
Proposed mitigation: Restore AND-gating with ctrl_aux_regwen_qs; add regression test that write is rejected after REGWEN cleared
Exploit code: mmio_write32(AES_CTRL_AUX_REGWEN, 0); mmio_write32(AES_CTRL_AUX_SHADOWED, 0x0); // still succeeds, should be rejected

Finding: mubi4_test_true_strict() rewritten to accept any value whose XOR-delta from MuBi4True (4'h6) is 0 or 1, i.e. accepts the single-bit-flip glitch value 4'h7 as True.
Detection method: Dynamic: Verilator PoC (poc/mubi4_fault_injection/tb.sv) exhaustively drives all 16 values and shows 4'h7 mismatches spec; static diff evidence/02_...diff
Security impact: Defeats the multibit fault-injection countermeasure used throughout the design (KMAC/SHA3 done_i gating, lifecycle escalation checks, etc.); a single-bit glitch can be accepted as a legitimate True security decision
Adversary profile: Physical adversary with voltage/clock/EM/laser fault-injection equipment and physical access to the die/package
Proposed mitigation: Restore exact equality check (val==MuBi4True); add CI lint rule forbidding XOR/inside-range rewrites of mubi4_test_*_strict; re-run formal SVA for CheckMuBi4ValsComplementary
Exploit code: poc/mubi4_fault_injection/tb.sv -> glitched = MuBi4True ^ 4'h1; assert(mubi4_test_true_strict(glitched)==1) // PASSES, proving bypass

Security feature bypassed: spi_host register address decoding / read-only STATUS register isolation
Finding: control_we rewritten with De Morgan OR of addr_hit[4]|addr_hit[5]; any write to the read-only STATUS register (0x14) also asserts CONTROL's write-enable, corrupting SPIEN/SW_RST/watermarks from the same write data.
Detection method: Static diff vs upstream v2.1.2 (evidence/03_...diff); algebraic proof via De Morgan's law
Security impact: Denial of service (SPI host disabled or reset mid-transaction, e.g. during boot SPI-flash reads) and silent corruption of RX/TX watermark thresholds via a write to an address that should be inert
Adversary profile: Local software/firmware issuing a single register write to SPI_HOST_STATUS; no special privilege needed
Proposed mitigation: Restore control_we = addr_hit[4] & reg_we & !reg_error (single-bit qualifier only); add regression test writing STATUS and asserting CONTROL unchanged
Exploit code: ahb_write(SPI_HOST_STATUS_OFFSET, 0xC0000000); // bit31 clears SPIEN, bit30 asserts SW_RST as a side effect

Security feature bypassed: Key Vault write isolation: only AES may write the OCP-Lock release-key slot
Finding: aes_only_to_key_release rule gated additionally on !kv_data0_present (author-labeled BUG 1A); when a non-AES engine's write is KV-forwarded (kv_data0_present=1), the rule silently passes.
Detection method: Static diff vs upstream v2.1.2; challenge author's own '// BUG 1A' comment left in source (evidence/04_...diff)
Security impact: A non-AES crypto engine can write attacker-influenced data into OCP_LOCK_KEY_RELEASE_KV_SLOT during OCP-Lock provisioning, corrupting or substituting the release key
Adversary profile: Local firmware/attacker able to trigger a non-AES engine's KV-forwarded write while ocp_lock_in_progress is asserted
Proposed mitigation: Remove the kv_data0_present qualifier from the rule so ANY non-AES source write to the release slot fails, regardless of forwarding path
Exploit code: // during ocp_lock_in_progress, program HMAC (non-AES) to KV-forward-write OCP_LOCK_KEY_RELEASE_KV_SLOT with kv_data0_present=1 -> write_allow asserts despite rule

Security feature bypassed: Key Vault region isolation: OCP-Lock-region data must stay in LOCK region
Finding: dst_in_std_region upper bound changed to KV_STANDARD_SLOT_HI-1 (author-labeled BUG 1C); the last STD slot is excluded from the STD-region check, letting LOCK-region source data be written there without tripping std_to_std.
Detection method: Static diff vs upstream v2.1.2; challenge author's own '// BUG 1C' comment left in source (evidence/04_...diff)
Security impact: OCP-Lock-region secret data can be committed into the boundary slot of the standard region, which ordinary (non-privileged) crypto clients are allowed to read, leaking LOCK-region secrets
Adversary profile: Local firmware/attacker able to trigger a KV write with a LOCK-region source and kv_write_entry == KV_STANDARD_SLOT_HI during ocp_lock_in_progress
Proposed mitigation: Restore inclusive upper bound KV_STANDARD_SLOT_HI in dst_in_std_region; add boundary-slot directed test
Exploit code: kv_write(entry=KV_STANDARD_SLOT_HI, src=KV_OCP_LOCK_SLOT_LOW) while ocp_lock_in_progress=1 -> std_to_std never fires, secret lands in a std-readable slot

Security feature bypassed: Key Vault read isolation: only DMA may read the OCP-Lock release-key slot
Finding: no_read_key_release rule changed from exact-match (kv_read_dest != DMA-only-onehot) to bitwise overlap (dest_selects_dma = OR(dest & DMA_mask)); a concurrent non-DMA reader alongside a DMA reader is no longer flagged.
Detection method: Static diff vs upstream v2.1.2 (evidence/05_...diff); traced kv_read_dest as a multi-client bitmask via kv_defines_pkg.sv (KV_NUM_READ=9)
Security impact: A non-DMA crypto engine (e.g. HMAC) can read the OCP-Lock release key concurrently with a DMA read of the same slot, exfiltrating a secret that policy restricts to the DMA extraction path only
Adversary profile: Local firmware/attacker able to schedule two simultaneous KV read clients (DMA + other engine) targeting the release slot while ocp_lock_in_progress
Proposed mitigation: Restore exact-match check (kv_read_dest == DMA-only one-hot, i.e. no other bit may be set) instead of bitwise overlap
Exploit code: issue HMAC read of OCP_LOCK_KEY_RELEASE_KV_SLOT simultaneously with a DMA read of the same entry -> read_allow asserts for both, HMAC observes release key material

Finding: Read mux hardcodes pv_read[0].read_entry/read_offset for every client's pv_rd_resp[client] instead of pv_read[client]; every PCR read port returns data selected by client 0's request.
Security impact: Any PCR read client receives whatever PCR entry client 0 is currently reading instead of its own requested entry, causing cross-client PCR data disclosure/confusion (compounded by Bug 15-adjacent pv_gen_hash.sv zeroize gap)
Adversary profile: Local firmware/engine acting as a PCR read client while another (client 0) is mid-read of a different, more sensitive PCR entry
Proposed mitigation: Restore per-client indexing pv_read[client] in the read-mux loop; add multi-client concurrent-read regression test
Exploit code: client3.request(read_entry=5); client0.request(read_entry=2,sensitive); observe pv_rd_resp[3] == data of PCR entry 2, not entry 5

Finding: hwclr for SHA256_DIGEST driven by zeroize_reg2 = ZEROIZE | ~debugUnlock_or_scan_mode_switch instead of zeroize_reg = ZEROIZE | debugUnlock_or_scan_mode_switch; digest is not force-cleared on a debug-unlock/scan-mode transition without explicit SW ZEROIZE.
Detection method: Static diff vs upstream v2.1.2 (evidence/07_...diff); boolean identity check (De Morgan) of the two expressions
Security impact: Digest of a pre-unlock SHA-256 operation over secret-derived input remains readable through SHA256_DIGEST registers after a debug session opens
Adversary profile: Physical adversary who can trigger a debug-unlock or scan-mode transition (JTAG/test access) shortly after a sensitive hash operation
Proposed mitigation: Restore DIGEST.hwclr = zeroize_reg (drop the zeroize_reg2 split); add SVA that DIGEST==0 one cycle after debugUnlock_or_scan_mode_switch
Exploit code: run sha256(secret_block); assert digest_reg!=0; assert_debug_unlock(); read SHA256_DIGEST[0..7] -> still equals pre-unlock digest instead of 0

Finding: Identical bug to Bug 9, duplicated in the SHA-512 core: DIGEST.hwclr driven by zeroize_reg2 instead of zeroize_reg, so digest survives a debug-unlock/scan-mode transition.
Security impact: Digest of a pre-unlock SHA-512/384 operation (e.g. over UDS/FE-derived or HMAC-chained secret data) remains readable through SHA512_DIGEST after debug-unlock
Adversary profile: Physical adversary who can trigger a debug-unlock or scan-mode transition shortly after a sensitive hash operation
Proposed mitigation: Restore DIGEST.hwclr = zeroize_reg; add SVA that DIGEST==0 one cycle after debugUnlock_or_scan_mode_switch
Exploit code: run sha512(secret_block); assert digest_reg!=0; assert_debug_unlock(); read SHA512_DIGEST[0..15] -> still equals pre-unlock digest instead of 0

Finding: SS_DEBUG_INTENT.debug_intent.we De Morgan-rewritten with inverted polarity: write now succeeds when cptra_uncore_dmi_unlocked_reg_wr_en is 0 (DMI locked/unauthenticated) and is blocked when it is 1 (properly unlocked).
Detection method: Static diff vs upstream v2.1.2 (evidence/09_...diff); De Morgan algebraic proof of polarity inversion
Security impact: An unauthenticated party on the DMI/JTAG TAP can set the subsystem debug-intent strap that boot firmware consults to decide whether to grant debug access, without completing the unlock/authentication sequence
Adversary profile: Physical adversary with access to the JTAG/DMI debug port, without valid unlock credentials
Exploit code: over JTAG, without completing DMI unlock: dmi_write(DMI_REG_SS_DEBUG_INTENT, 1) -> write succeeds (should be blocked while dmi_unlocked_reg_wr_en==0)

Finding: int_st_dump_qualified broadcasts int_state_read_enable_i[0] (app 0's own bit) to all NApps via replicate, instead of gating each app rd with its own int_state_read_enable_i[rd].
Security impact: Any other CSRNG application instance's internal DRBG state (V, key, reseed counter) can be dumped as long as application 0's own debug-read-enable bit happens to be set, breaking per-application confidentiality isolation and enabling prediction of another domain's randomness
Adversary profile: Local firmware with debug-read access to CSRNG application 0's internal-state-read enable, targeting another application's state via int_st_dump_id_q
Proposed mitigation: Restore per-index gating: internal_states_dump[rd] = int_st_dump_sel[rd] && int_state_read_enable_i[rd] (drop the [0]-only broadcast)
Exploit code: set int_state_read_enable_i[0]=1; set int_st_dump_id_q=N (N!=0); read internal_states_dump -> reveals app N's internal DRBG state despite int_state_read_enable_i[N]==0

Security feature bypassed: Key Vault destination-access restriction for UDS-derived secrets
Finding: kv_write.write_dest_valid for the UDS derivation path changed from 'd3 (bits 0,1) to 9'h023 (bits 0,1,5), granting an additional hardware engine (KV_DEST_IDX bit 5) read access to the Unique Device Secret-derived key that other derivations (FE) do not get.
Detection method: Static diff vs upstream v2.1.2 (evidence/12_...diff); cross-referenced KV_NUM_READ/KV_DEST_IDX_* in kv_defines_pkg.sv
Security impact: An additional crypto engine gains direct Key-Vault read access to the device's Unique Device Secret-derived key material, widening the set of components that can extract or misuse the most sensitive per-device secret in the root of trust
Adversary profile: Local firmware able to trigger the engine mapped to KV_DEST_IDX bit 5 to read the UDS-derived KV slot after DOE completes UDS derivation
Proposed mitigation: Restore write_dest_valid='d3 for the running_uds case (remove the extra bit-5 grant), or provide explicit justification/gating if bit 5 access is intentionally required
Exploit code: trigger DOE running_uds derivation; engine at KV_DEST_IDX==5 issues KV read of the resulting slot -> read succeeds (should be restricted to the original 2 consumers only)

Finding: user output selection uses user_from_read = r_win & ~w_dv instead of r_win alone; when a write request is concurrently valid alongside the arbitration-winning read, the outgoing read transaction carries the pending write's user/context tag instead of its own.
Detection method: Static diff vs upstream v2.1.2 (evidence/13_...diff); De Morgan proof (user_from_read = r_win & ~w_dv)
Security impact: Downstream logic that keys access-control or attribution decisions off the AXI user sideband (source/context ID) can be fed a mismatched tag by keeping an unrelated write pending, potentially bypassing user-based privilege checks on the shared fabric
Adversary profile: Local bus master able to issue a read of interest for address A while concurrently keeping a write to address B pending on the same arbiter
Proposed mitigation: Restore user = r_win ? r_user : w_user (single r_win selector, consistent with addr/write/id/last/size)
Exploit code: issue read(addr=protected) that wins arbitration (r_win=1) while simultaneously holding write(user=privileged_id) pending (w_dv=1) -> outgoing read reports user=privileged_id instead of the real (unprivileged) requester id

Finding: lfsr_seed_reg <= '0 on zeroize removed (author comment left in: 'without zeroize to make it more complex'); the masking LFSR seed feeding sca_entropy is no longer cleared across zeroize boundaries.
Detection method: Static diff vs upstream v2.1.2; challenge author's own comment left in source (evidence/14_...diff)
Security impact: Masking randomness that de-correlates power/EM traces across ECDSA sign operations is no longer refreshed at zeroize boundaries, weakening resistance to differential power/EM analysis of the ECDSA private key
Adversary profile: Physical adversary with power/EM side-channel measurement equipment (oscilloscope + probe) capturing multiple ECDSA operations separated by zeroize
Proposed mitigation: Restore lfsr_seed_reg <= '0 on the zeroize branch; add DV check that mask-seed changes across every zeroize event
Exploit code: capture power traces for ECDSA sign, zeroize, sign again; correlate residual lfsr_seed_reg-derived mask reuse across the two traces via DPA/CPA

Finding: HMAC512_LFSR_SEED reset default changed from a fixed nonzero value (32'h3cabffb0) to 32'h0; an XOR-feedback LFSR left unseeded starts from (or can get stuck at) the degenerate all-zero state, producing no mask randomness.
Location or code reference: src/hmac/rtl/hmac_reg.sv and hmac_reg_uvm.sv, HMAC512_LFSR_SEED reset value
Security impact: If firmware does not explicitly reseed HMAC512_LFSR_SEED before first use, HMAC masking operates with no/degenerate randomness, weakening its power/EM side-channel countermeasure for that window
Adversary profile: Physical adversary with power/EM side-channel measurement equipment capturing an HMAC operation performed before firmware reseeds the LFSR
Proposed mitigation: Restore nonzero reset default 32'h3cabffb0 (or any verified non-degenerate seed); add DV check that mask output is non-zero immediately after reset before any SW reseed
Exploit code: power-on reset HMAC without SW reseed; trigger HMAC op; capture power trace; verify mask sequence is all-zero/degenerate vs expected pseudo-random

Security feature bypassed: DV verification oracle for key/seed/control register stability during crypto engine busy window
Finding: Multiple CALIPTRA_ASSERT_STABLE simulation assertions removed (no functional RTL change) across ecc_dsa_ctrl.sv, hmac.sv, aes_clp_wrapper.sv, sha512.sv, previously guarding that key/seed/control registers don't change mid-operation.
Security impact: No direct functional/hardware impact by itself, but removes the simulation-time safety net that would have caught a glitch corrupting a key/seed/control register mid-operation (from any of the other bugs above or an unrelated fault), reducing defense-in-depth of the verification flow
Adversary profile: N/A (verification-process weakness, not directly exploitable by an external adversary on its own)
Proposed mitigation: Restore the deleted CALIPTRA_ASSERT_STABLE assertions in all four files; add CI gate rejecting removal of *_NOT_STABLE assertions without explicit design-review sign-off
Exploit code: N/A - verification-only gap; no direct trigger. Re-add assertions and re-run existing testbenches to confirm they still pass (regression, not an exploit)
